newsitem.title: GERMANY: Meister urges long-term deficit-cutting measures.
newsitem.headline: Meister urges long-term deficit-cutting measures.

text.p: Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister on Tuesday urged countries to take long-term measures to reduce their budget deficits and not aim purely at hitting the three percent level referred to in the Maastricht Treaty.

"Many European countries are facing problems in taking the three percent hurdle, even if one does not insist that it be met exactly," he said in the text of a speech to be delivered to a conference in Kaernten, Austria.
European countries are required to cut their budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product this year if they want to join the euro at is planned launch in 1999.
"In Germany, the prospects for budget developments are now less favourable than was assumed a few months ago," Meister said according to a text of his speech released in advance of delivery.
"Growth is below expectations and falling tax income, together with higher joblessness meant the three percent mark appears harder to reach."
He added that this meant there could be no abandonment of consolidation measures.
"It would be more important to take measures which will have a long-term effect that to achieve a direct hit which is only achieved through one-off measures," he said.
Meister said long-term convergence would be important for the long-term success of the single currency. He added that correct application of the stability pact would also be key.
